abstract: Background: Tensor-decomposition-based unsupervised feature extraction (TD-based UFE) selects genes by attributing P-values to the components of a gene singular vector under a null normal distribution. The standard deviation sigma of this distribution is unknown and is chosen so that the histogram of the P-values of the genes that are not selected becomes as flat as possible. This heuristic has worked well in practice but has had no theoretical justification. Results: We prove, for a model of signal, mean expression and noise, that the higher-order singular value decomposition has a component that reproduces the experimental design, that the components of its gene singular vector belonging to background genes are approximately normal with standard deviation sigma_0 = sqrt(d)/s, where d is the noise variance and s the singular value, and that signal genes separate from the background even when they form a positive fraction of all genes. We derive the limit of the objective function of the flattening and prove, by a computer-assisted argument based on interval arithmetic, that for 100 histogram bins, Benjamini-Hochberg level 0.01 and every fraction of background genes between 0.1 and 0.99, the limit has a unique minimizer within 1.1% of sigma_0. We formalize the practice of taking the valley to the right of the peak of the objective as a maximum-drop rule and prove that the resulting estimator is consistent up to this bounded bias. Conclusions: Flattening the P-value histogram estimates the noise level of the background genes, with a small and bounded systematic bias, provided that the signals are strong enough to be detected individually and that the noise variances of background genes are nearly equal.

title: Why flattening the P-value histogram works: a theory of the standard-deviation optimization in tensor-decomposition-based unsupervised feature extraction
